extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers interested in crowd psychology and social influence
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing Le Bon's criteria and conceptual dimensions about prestige, fixed beliefs, and changeable opinions in crowds — how prestige arises, operates, and decays, and how collective beliefs form and change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of prestige
rubrics_metrics.description: Prestige is a domination exercised on our mind by an individual, a work, or an idea that paralyses critical faculty and fills the soul with astonishment and respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prestige produces an inexplicable fascination (compared to magnetisation). It can be possessed by the dead or fictive beings; it need not be based on personal admiration or fear. Examples: Alexander, Caesar, Buddha; monstrous divinities may have prestige without being admired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prestige as the mainspring of authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Prestige is the fundamental source of all authority; gods, kings, and leaders rely on it to reign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority rests on the crowd's acceptance produced by prestige rather than on formal structures alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquired (artificial) prestige
rubrics_metrics.description: Prestige resulting from name, fortune, reputation, position, titles, or dress; it may be independent of the individual's personal worth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniforms, robes, decorations, titles, and social position confer prestige (e.g., soldiers in uniform, judges in robes). This form is common and can be entirely superficial — someone with little intrinsic merit may enjoy prestige due to external trappings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal (magnetic) prestige
rubrics_metrics.description: A quality intrinsic to some individuals that enables them to exert a veritable magnetic fascination and compel acceptance of their ideas without formal authority or titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal prestige can exist absent reputation or fortune and explains leadership of figures like Buddha, Jesus, Muhammad, Joan of Arc, Napoleon. Such prestige resists discussion and forces obedience akin to a tamer's control over wild animals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prestige of works and opinions via repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary or artistic prestige often arises from accumulated repetitions of identical judgments (tradition), causing names and works to become unquestioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical repetition and unverified transmission (e.g., schooling) build prestige for works (Homer, Parthenon) that may no longer merit it on direct inspection; prestige prevents seeing things as they really are.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of prestige on judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Prestige paralyses judgment and prevents observers from seeing things as they truly are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prestige causes people to adopt ready-made opinions regardless of truth or falsity; crowds and most individuals rely on these prepackaged judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation and contagion as outcomes of prestige
rubrics_metrics.description: An object, person, or idea possessing prestige is immediately imitated by others through contagion, often unconsciously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artists and writers adopt styles popularised by prestigious figures without recognizing the origin of their inspiration; imitation tends to be perfect and unconscious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Success as a principal source of prestige
rubrics_metrics.description: Success is a key factor in generating prestige: every successful person or idea that forces recognition tends to escape questioning and gain prestige.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prestige typically increases with success and tends to vanish with failure. The stronger the prior prestige, the more violent the reaction when failure occurs (crowd revenge on fallen heroes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prestige decay via failure and discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Prestige disappears rapidly after failure and is more slowly worn away but certainly destroyed when subjected to discussion or questioning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loss of success quickly strips prestige; public debate undermines prestige because the admired must be kept at a distance to maintain awe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Range of prestige (spectrum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prestige exists on a continuum from founders of religions and empires to trivial social status signals (e.g., new coat, decoration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extreme cases (religious founders, emperors) sit at one end, private social affectation at the other; many intermediate forms arise from elements of civilisation (science, art, literature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed (general) beliefs — permanence and role
rubrics_metrics.description: Great generalised beliefs endure for centuries, form the real framework of civilisation, shape institutions, arts, and modes of existence, and are very difficult to uproot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: feudalism, Christianity, Protestantism, nationalism. Such beliefs determine trends of ideas, inspire faith and duty, and changing them generally requires violent revolutions or long decay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intolerance as a social virtue for maintaining beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: Nations display intolerance to defend general beliefs; although philosophically open to criticism, intolerance functions as a necessary virtue for peoples to found and uphold cohesive beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical intolerance (e.g., persecution in the Middle Ages) is explained as instrumental to implanting and preserving beliefs that underpin civilisation; innovators often suffer for challenging established beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophic absurdity does not prevent belief spread
rubrics_metrics.description: The logical absurdity of a belief is not an obstacle to its widespread acceptance and endurance among crowds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious legends that are philosophically barbarous may nonetheless shape civilisation for centuries (e.g., doctrines accepted despite being absurd on philosophical grounds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Changeable (transitory) opinions — nature and contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: Above fixed beliefs lie ephemeral opinions and fashions that arise and vanish rapidly, often unconnected to the deeper characteristic beliefs of a race.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literary and artistic movements (romanticism, naturalism, mysticism) are examples. Such opinions are compared to ripples on a lake — superficial and often transient within a generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes increasing volatility of opinions in modern times
rubrics_metrics.description: Three modern causes expand the number of changeable opinions: erosion of old general beliefs, increased power of crowds, and development of the newspaper press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weakening of foundational beliefs leaves space for capricious opinions; stronger crowds can express mobility of ideas; newspapers continually present contradictory opinions, preventing any single opinion from stabilising widely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press as reflector rather than director of opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The modern press largely reflects the opinions and fluctuations of crowds instead of directing them, becoming an agency for information and entertainment rather than a shaper of convictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers must follow changing tastes to retain readers; literary and theatrical critics have lost power to ensure success and may only harm; old influential organs have declined into news-and-gossip formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governments powerless to direct modern opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Statesmen and governments no longer reliably direct public opinion; instead they often follow it because of fear of popular reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governments monitor public opinion constantly; policy and alliances (e.g., Franco-Russian alliance example) can be driven by popular movements rather than elite direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency of crowds toward indifference and divergent convictions
rubrics_metrics.description: The combined effects of weakened general beliefs and volatile opinions produce extreme divergence of convictions and growing indifference among crowds toward matters not directly affecting their immediate interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doctrinal questions (e.g., socialism) mainly recruit the genuinely convinced from less-educated classes; on many other topics crowds show indifference unless personally impacted.
